{{Short description|Absorbing boundary condition for wave problems}}
[[File:Mur absorbing boundary condition in 1D FDTD.gif|thumb|Demonstration of Mur absorbing boundary condition in a 1D finite-difference time-domain simulation|300px]]
In [[numerical methods for partial differential equations]], '''Engquist–Majda absorbing boundary conditions''' or '''Lindman–Engquist–Majda absorbing boundary conditions''' are a hierarchy of [[absorbing boundary condition]]s for the numerical solution of [[wave equation]]s. Named after mathematicians [[Björn Engquist]] and [[Andrew Majda]], they are designed to allow waves to exit a finite computational domain with minimal artificial [[Reflection (physics)|reflection]] through the use of [[one-way wave equation]]s, essentially making the boundaries transparent to outgoing [[radiation]]. Within the context of [[computational electromagnetics]], they are known as '''Mur absorbing boundary condition''' after Gerrit Mur, who introduced a discretized version of the boundary conditions for [[finite-difference time-domain method]]  in 1981.

==Theory==
A simple form of Engquist–Majda absorbing boundary condition can be formulated through one-dimensional scalar wave equation:<ref name="taflove2005"/>
:<math>\left(L_x^2- v^{-2} L_t^2\right) U(x,t)=G U(x,t)=0</math>
where <math>L_{\{x,t\}}=\partial_{\{x,t\}}</math> are the partial [[differential operator]]s and <math>v</math> is the [[Wave#Wave velocity|wave velocity]]; <math>G</math> is the resultant wave function operator. This operator can be split into two [[One-way wave equation|one-way wave operators]], resulting in [[advection]] equations:
:<math>G U(x,t)=G^+ G^- U(x,t)=0</math>
:<math>G^+=L_x+v^{-1} L_t</math>
:<math>G^-=L_x-v^{-1} L_t</math>
Applying the following boundary conditions at a simulation region from <math>x=0</math> to <math>x=L</math> results in the cancellation of outgoing waves:
:<math>G^+ U(x,t)|_{x=0}=\left(L_x+v^{-1} L_t\right)U(x,t)|_{x=0}=0</math>
:<math>G^- U(x,t)|_{x=L}=\left(L_x-v^{-1} L_t\right)U(x,t)|_{x=L}=0</math>

In the case of higher dimensions, i.e. the two-dimensional scalar wave equation, the operator form can be written as:<ref name="engquist1977"/>
:<math>\left(L_x^2+L_y^2 - v^{-2} L_t^2\right) U(x,y,t)=G^+ G^- U(x,y,t)=0</math>
For waves traveling along the <math>x</math>-axis, the operator splitting results in:
:<math>G^+ U(x,y,t)|_{x=0}=\left(L_x+v^{-1} L_t \sqrt{1 - v^{2}\frac{L_y^2}{L_t^2}}\right)U(x,t)|_{x=0}=0</math>
:<math>G^- U(x,y,t)|_{x=L}=\left(L_x-v^{-1} L_t \sqrt{1 - v^{2}\frac{L_y^2}{L_t^2}}\right)U(x,t)|_{x=L}=0</math>
The terms in square brackets constitute [[pseudo-differential operator]]s and their theoretical exact forms are [[nonlocal operator|nonlocal]]. In practice, they can be locally approximated with their [[Taylor series]] representations. First-order approximation <math>(\sqrt{1-s^2} \approx 1)</math> yields:
:<math>G^+ \approx L_x+v^{-1} L_t </math>
:<math>G^- \approx L_x-v^{-1} L_t </math>
which is equivalent to the Engquist–Majda condition for one-dimensional wave equation: in the theoretical limit, it perfectly absorbs the normally incident waves while causing reflections for waves impinging on other angles. A second-order approximation <math>(\sqrt{1-s^2} \approx 1-s^2/2)</math> yields a better performance:
:<math>G^+ \approx L_x+v^{-1} L_t \left[1-v^{2}\frac{L_y^2}{2 L_t^2}\right]=L_x+v^{-1} L_t-\frac{v^2 L_y^2}{2L_t^2}</math>
:<math>G^- \approx L_x-v^{-1} L_t \left[1-v^{2}\frac{L_y^2}{2 L_t^2}\right]=L_x-v^{-1} L_t+\frac{v^2 L_y^2}{2L_t^2}</math>

Higher-order boundary conditions can also be obtained through [[Padé approximation|Padé]] or [[Chebyshev polynomials|Chebyshev approximation]] of the pseudo-differential operators;<ref name="trefethen1986"/><ref name="halpern1988"/> these are known as generalized Trefethen–Halpern absorbing boundary conditions.<ref name="taflove2005"/>

==History and applications==
Engquist and Majda's seminal paper on the absorbing boundary conditions was published in 1977.<ref name="engquist1977"/> An earlier form of the absorbing boundary conditions was previously reported in 1973 by physicist and [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] staff member Erick L. Lindman,<ref name="lindman1973"/><ref name="lindman1975"/> who first suggested the use of one-way equations to construct absorbing boundaries.<ref name="kausel1988"/> Since their introduction, Engquist–Majda absorbing boundary conditions have been applied to numerical solutions of various different problems in areas ranging from [[acoustics]] to [[seismology]], particularly within [[Finite difference method|finite difference]] and [[Finite element method|finite element]] formulations.<ref name="clayton1977"/><ref name="shubin1987"/><ref name="hadley1992"/><ref name="ihlenburg1998"/><ref name="komatitsch1998"/> In [[computational electromagnetics]], they are known as Mur boundary conditions, named after Gerrit Mur's extension of the Engquist–Majda operators to the [[finite-difference time-domain method]] (FDTD).<ref name="mur1981"/> While Mur boundary condition enjoyed popularity in the FDTD applications for a decade following its introduction, it was subsequently superseded by more efficient [[perfectly matched layer]]s<ref name="berenger2022"/> and more accurate exact absorbing conditions<ref name="sirenko2011"/> in the 1990s.

Engquist–Majda absorbing boundary conditions, alongside the [[Dirac equation]], were instrumental in the development of an exact one-way wave equation in 2025.<ref name="tsakmakidis2025"/>
